domain: Criminal Justice / Political Philosophy / Legal Theory
topic_summary: Analysis of capital punishment as a contested kernel where the state-killing commitment is read through three incompatible frameworks: retributive justice (desert-based execution), deterrence (instrumental crime prevention), and abolition (categorical impermissibility). Each reading instantiates a structurally different constraint with distinct beneficiary/victim configurations and authority groundings.

key_entities: State execution apparatus (prosecutors, courts, corrections systems)
Abolitionist movement (Beccaria lineage, human rights framework)
Innocent persons at risk of wrongful execution
key_tensions: Victim family interests vs state prosecution interests (families divided; prosecutors assume unanimity)
Empirical deterrence claims vs null findings (NRC review vs pro-deterrence studies)
Retributive desert vs human rights inviolability (proportionality vs categorical prohibition)
Cost of capital litigation vs alternative crime prevention (resource allocation)
Irreversible error risk vs claimed moral necessity (innocence vs desert)
key_mechanisms: Deterrence signaling (threatened execution prevents future murders)
Closure provision for families (contested empirical claim)
Human rights treaty obligations (abolitionist legal architecture)
key_absences: Racial disparities in death sentencing (not addressed in research context)
International law pressure on retentionist states (mentioned but not analyzed)
Victim family agency in sentencing decisions (families excluded from process despite being invoked)

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Three readings selected represent structurally distinct constraint instantiations with different authority groundings, beneficiary/victim structures, and observables. Deferred axes documented as downstream or internal to selected readings.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: State authority to intentionally kill condemned persons as legitimate exercise of sovereign power
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Mixed: retributive (Kantian desert), utilitarian (consequentialist crime prevention), human rights (categorical dignity)

readings.commitment: Murderer forfeits life-right through proportional desert (lex talionis)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Offender enters victim set as morally deserving; society/moral order as beneficiary; high ε from desert-based legitimacy

readings.commitment: Execution justified as rational signal preventing future murders
readings.expected_structural_delta: Offender instrumentalized as means to social end; potential future victims as beneficiary; moderate ε from contested empirical evidence

readings.commitment: State killing categorically violates human dignity regardless of desert or utility
readings.expected_structural_delta: Condemned person as rights-bearer beneficiary; state killing power itself as victim; high ε from categorical prohibition

axiom_contradictions.basis: Retributive axiom (proportional desert can mandate death) and abolitionist axiom (human dignity categorically prohibits intentional state killing) cannot coexist in a single coherent normative framework. Accepting abolition's categorical prohibition requires rejecting desert as sufficient justification.

Deterrence axiom (consequentialist utility can justify killing as means) and abolitionist axiom (human dignity prohibits instrumentalization unto death) cannot coexist. Accepting abolition's categorical prohibition requires rejecting utilitarian instrumentalization as legitimate.
